I. Causes cutaneous photosensitivity
II. Is the rarest of the porphyrias
III. Is caused by porphobilinogen deaminase deficiency
questions.why: Only I is true; it is the commonest porphyria and is due to uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency.

questions.stem:
Sources of haem for catabolism include:
I. Haemoglobin from senescent red cells
II. Cytochrome P450 and other haem proteins
III. Haem from ineffective erythropoiesis
questions.why: All three contribute to the haem that is catabolised.

questions.stem:
ALA dehydratase (porphobilinogen synthase):
I. Converts porphobilinogen to hydroxymethylbilane
II. Requires zinc for activity
III. Is inhibited by lead
questions.why: II and III are true; it condenses two ALA to form PBG (not PBG to HMB), so I is false.

questions.stem: All of the following are haem-containing proteins EXCEPT:
questions.why: Creatine kinase is not a haem protein; the others all contain haem.

questions.stem: All of the following enzymes act in the haem SYNTHESIS pathway EXCEPT:
questions.why: Biliverdin reductase belongs to haem catabolism, not synthesis.

questions.stem: All of the following are true of haem oxygenase EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: it requires zinc as a cofactor

options.label: D
options.text: it uses haem as its substrate

questions.why: Zinc is the cofactor of ALA dehydratase, not haem oxygenase.

questions.stem: All of the following occur in lead poisoning EXCEPT:
questions.why: Lead reduces haem synthesis; the de-repression raises ALA but output falls.

questions.stem: All of the following cause predominantly UNCONJUGATED hyperbilirubinaemia EXCEPT:

options.label: C
options.text: gallstone obstruction of the bile duct

questions.why: Bile-duct obstruction is post-hepatic and raises CONJUGATED bilirubin.

questions.stem: All of the following are features of the porphyrias EXCEPT:

options.label: C
options.text: an enzyme defect in the haem pathway

options.label: D
options.text: a complete absence of haem synthesis

questions.why: Some haem is still made (≈50% enzyme activity); synthesis is not absent.

questions.stem: The rate-limiting enzyme of haem biosynthesis is:
questions.why: ALA synthase catalyses the committed, rate-limiting step.

questions.stem: Haem synthesis begins with the condensation of glycine with:
questions.why: Glycine condenses with succinyl-CoA to form ALA.

questions.stem: The porphyrin found combined with iron in haem is:
questions.why: Haem is ferroprotoporphyrin IX - protoporphyrin IX plus ferrous iron.

questions.stem: The enzyme that inserts iron into protoporphyrin IX is:
questions.why: Ferrochelatase (haem synthase) inserts Fe2+ into protoporphyrin IX.

questions.stem: The only endogenous source of carbon monoxide is the reaction catalysed by:
questions.why: Haem oxygenase releases CO as it opens the haem ring.

questions.stem: Unconjugated bilirubin is made water-soluble in the liver by conjugation with:
questions.why: UDP-glucuronyl transferase conjugates bilirubin with glucuronic acid.

questions.stem: The enzyme deficient in acute intermittent porphyria is:
questions.why: AIP results from porphobilinogen deaminase deficiency.

questions.stem: Kernicterus in the newborn results from brain deposition of:
questions.why: Lipophilic unconjugated bilirubin crosses the immature blood-brain barrier.

questions.stem: In the intestine, bacteria convert bilirubin into the colourless compound:
questions.why: Gut bacteria reduce bilirubin to colourless urobilinogen (stercobilinogen).

questions.stem: The enzyme deficient in porphyria cutanea tarda is:
questions.why: PCT is due to uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Myoglobin has a higher oxygen affinity than haemoglobin at low oxygen tensions.
Reason: Myoglobin binds oxygen non-cooperatively whereas haemoglobin binds cooperatively.
questions.why: Non-cooperative binding gives myoglobin its hyperbolic, high-affinity curve, explaining the difference.

questions.stem:
Assertion: 2,3-BPG lowers the oxygen affinity of haemoglobin.
Reason: 2,3-BPG binds in the central cavity and stabilises the deoxy (T) state.
questions.why: Stabilising the T state is exactly how BPG reduces oxygen affinity.

questions.stem:
Assertion: A fall in pH shifts the haemoglobin oxygen dissociation curve to the right.
Reason: A lowered pH reduces haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen (the Bohr effect).
questions.why: The right shift is the reduced affinity the Bohr effect produces.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Fetal haemoglobin has a higher oxygen affinity than adult HbA.
Reason: Fetal haemoglobin binds 2,3-BPG less strongly than adult haemoglobin.
questions.why: Weaker BPG binding leaves fetal Hb with higher oxygen affinity, aiding placental transfer.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Haemoglobin A is composed of two alpha and two beta chains.
Reason: The beta chain contains 146 amino acids.
questions.why: Both are true, but the chain length does not explain the subunit composition.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Thalassaemia is common in malaria-endemic regions.
Reason: Thalassaemia results from reduced synthesis of a globin chain.
questions.why: Both true, but the molecular defect does not explain the geographic (malarial) distribution.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin more tightly than oxygen does.
Reason: The distal histidine forces bound carbon monoxide into a bent configuration.
questions.why: Both true, but the bent configuration reduces CO affinity - it does not explain why CO still out-binds O2.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Only ferrous (Fe2+) haemoglobin can bind oxygen.
Reason: Methaemoglobin contains iron in the ferrous (Fe2+) state.
questions.why: Only Fe2+ binds O2, but methaemoglobin is the ferric (Fe3+) form, so the reason is false.

questions.stem:
Assertion: In beta-thalassaemia major, HbF is markedly increased.
Reason: The beta-globin genes are normal in beta-thalassaemia major.
questions.why: HbF does rise, but the beta genes are defective - that is the disease - so the reason is false.

questions.stem:
Assertion: The proximal histidine binds directly to the haem iron.
Reason: It occupies the sixth coordination position of the iron atom.
questions.why: The proximal histidine binds iron at the FIFTH position; the sixth binds oxygen, so the reason is false.

questions.stem:
Assertion: 2,3-BPG binds to the alpha chains of haemoglobin.
Reason: 2,3-BPG stabilises the deoxygenated form of haemoglobin.
questions.why: BPG binds the BETA chains (assertion false); it does stabilise deoxyhaemoglobin (reason true).

questions.stem:
Assertion: HbH disease results from deletion of all four alpha-globin genes.
Reason: Haemoglobin H is a tetramer of beta chains (β4).
questions.why: HbH disease is three-gene deletion (assertion false); HbH is indeed β4 (reason true).

questions.stem:
Assertion: Oxygen binding by myoglobin is strongly regulated by pH and pCO2.
Reason: Haemoglobin shows cooperative oxygen binding.
questions.why: Myoglobin binding is NOT affected by pH/CO2 (assertion false); haemoglobin is cooperative (reason true).

questions.stem:
Assertion: Haemoglobin binds oxygen along a hyperbolic dissociation curve.
Reason: Haemoglobin does not show cooperativity.
questions.why: Haemoglobin's curve is sigmoid and it is cooperative; both statements are false.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Bart's hydrops fetalis is a mild condition compatible with normal life.
Reason: Haemoglobin Bart's (γ4) is an efficient oxygen carrier.
questions.why: Bart's hydrops is lethal and γ4 is a useless oxygen carrier; both false.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Beta-thalassaemia is usually caused by large deletions of the beta gene.
Reason: Alpha-thalassaemia is usually caused by point mutations.
questions.why: It is the reverse: beta-thal is mostly point mutations and alpha-thal mostly deletions; both false.

questions.stem:
The following are true of myoglobin:
I. It is a monomeric protein
II. It stores oxygen in muscle
III. It binds oxygen through a haem group
questions.why: All three are correct.

questions.stem:
Concerning 2,3-BPG:
I. It lowers haemoglobin oxygen affinity
II. It binds in the central cavity between the beta chains
III. It binds fetal haemoglobin more strongly than adult HbA
questions.why: I and II true; it binds fetal Hb LESS strongly, so III is false.

questions.stem:
The Bohr effect in haemoglobin:
I. Affects oxygen binding by myoglobin to the same degree
II. Causes a right shift of the curve when pH falls
III. Causes a right shift of the curve when pCO2 rises
questions.why: II and III true; myoglobin is unaffected by pH/CO2, so I is false.

questions.stem:
Haemoglobin A:
I. Contains two alpha and two beta chains
II. Has alpha chains of 146 amino acids
III. Carries H+ and CO2 as well as oxygen
questions.why: I and III true; the alpha chain has 141 (beta has 146) amino acids, so II is false.

questions.stem:
Methaemoglobin:
I. Contains ferric (Fe3+) iron
II. Binds oxygen normally
III. Is the predominant form in arterial blood
questions.why: Only I is true; ferric Hb cannot bind oxygen and is normally a tiny fraction.

questions.stem:
In beta-thalassaemia major (Cooley's anaemia):
I. HbA is absent or very low
II. HbF is markedly increased
III. Lifelong transfusions are usually needed
questions.why: All three are characteristic.

questions.stem:
The alpha-thalassaemias:
I. Involve genes on chromosome 16
II. Are usually caused by gene deletions
III. Are never clinically severe
questions.why: I and II true; deletion of all four genes (Bart's) is lethal, so III is false.

questions.stem:
HbH disease:
I. Is caused by deletion of all four alpha genes
II. Features a β4 tetramer (haemoglobin H)
III. Produces a haemolytic anaemia
questions.why: II and III true; it is a THREE-gene deletion, so I is false.

questions.stem:
In the haem group of haemoglobin:
I. Iron is held by the four pyrrole nitrogens
II. The proximal histidine binds at the sixth coordination position
III. Oxygen binds at the sixth coordination position
questions.why: I and III true; the proximal histidine binds at the FIFTH position, so II is false.

questions.stem:
Fetal haemoglobin:
I. Has a higher oxygen affinity than HbA
II. Has the composition alpha-2 beta-2
III. Binds 2,3-BPG more strongly than HbA
questions.why: Only I is true; fetal Hb is α2γ2 and binds BPG weakly.

questions.stem:
Ineffective erythropoiesis in thalassaemia involves:
I. Precipitation of unmatched globin chains
II. Damage to red-cell membranes
III. Haemolysis of red cells within the marrow
questions.why: All three describe the ineffective erythropoiesis of thalassaemia.

questions.stem:
Beta-thalassaemia minor (trait):
I. Shows an HbA2 below the normal range
II. Causes a mild, well-tolerated anaemia
III. Is often mistaken for iron-deficiency anaemia
questions.why: II and III true; HbA2 is RAISED (>3.5%), so I is false.

questions.stem: All of the following are true of myoglobin EXCEPT:

options.label: C
options.text: it has a hyperbolic oxygen curve

questions.why: Myoglobin is monomeric and cannot bind cooperatively; haemoglobin does that.

questions.stem: All of the following cause a LEFT shift of the oxygen dissociation curve EXCEPT:
questions.why: A rise in 2,3-BPG lowers affinity and shifts the curve to the RIGHT.

questions.stem: All of the following are features of beta-thalassaemia major EXCEPT:

options.label: B
options.text: severe anaemia in the first year

questions.why: Electrophoresis is grossly abnormal (HbA absent, HbF high).

questions.stem: All of the following stabilise the deoxy (T) state of haemoglobin EXCEPT:
questions.why: Oxygen binding breaks the T-state bonds and drives the switch to the R state.

questions.stem: All of the following are true of the alpha-thalassaemias EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: loss of all four genes is lethal

options.label: B
options.text: loss of three genes causes HbH disease

options.label: C
options.text: they are usually caused by point mutations

options.label: E
options.text: they are usually caused by deletions

questions.why: Alpha-thalassaemia is mostly due to gene DELETIONS, not point mutations.

questions.stem: All of the following are used in the treatment of beta-thalassaemia major EXCEPT:
questions.why: Venesection would worsen the anaemia; iron is removed by chelation, not bleeding.

questions.stem: The quaternary structure of normal adult haemoglobin (HbA) is:
questions.why: HbA is two alpha and two beta chains (α2β2).

questions.stem: The residue occupying the fifth coordination position of the haem iron is the:
questions.why: The proximal histidine (F8) binds the iron directly at the fifth position.

questions.stem: Oxygen binds to haemoglobin only when the iron is in the:
questions.why: Only ferrous (Fe2+) iron binds oxygen; the ferric form is methaemoglobin.

questions.stem: The shape of the haemoglobin oxygen dissociation curve is:
questions.why: Cooperative binding gives haemoglobin a sigmoid curve (myoglobin's is hyperbolic).

questions.stem: The intracellular compound that chiefly lowers the oxygen affinity of haemoglobin is:
questions.why: 2,3-BPG binds deoxyhaemoglobin and lowers its oxygen affinity.

questions.stem: Fetal haemoglobin (HbF) has the chain composition:
questions.why: HbF is two alpha and two gamma chains (α2γ2).

questions.stem: Haemoglobin Bart's, seen in the lethal alpha-thalassaemia syndrome, is a tetramer of:
questions.why: With no alpha chains made, gamma chains form the γ4 tetramer, Hb Bart's.

questions.stem: A raised HbA2 (above 3.5%) is the characteristic laboratory finding in:
questions.why: A raised HbA2 distinguishes beta-thalassaemia trait from iron deficiency.

questions.stem: The iron-chelating drug used to prevent iron overload in thalassaemia major is:
questions.why: Desferrioxamine chelates and removes the iron that accumulates with transfusion.

questions.stem: The distal histidine (E7) of myoglobin and haemoglobin reduces the binding of:
questions.why: The distal histidine bends and weakens CO binding, protecting against poisoning.

questions.stem:
Assertion: In galactosaemia a cataract develops.
Reason: Galactose is reduced to galactitol, which accumulates osmotically in the lens.
questions.why: Galactitol accumulation in the lens is exactly how the cataract forms.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency raises urinary orotic acid.
Reason: Carbamoyl phosphate that cannot enter the urea cycle is diverted into pyrimidine (orotic acid) synthesis.
questions.why: The diverted carbamoyl phosphate is why orotic acid rises - the reason explains the finding.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Urea cycle defects cause hyperammonaemia.
Reason: The urea cycle is the main route for converting waste nitrogen into urea.
questions.why: Blocking the cycle leaves ammonia undisposed, so the reason explains the hyperammonaemia.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Phenylketonuria causes hypopigmentation of skin and hair.
Reason: Reduced formation of tyrosine limits melanin synthesis.
questions.why: Low tyrosine (and high phenylalanine inhibiting tyrosinase) reduces melanin, explaining the pallor.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Inborn errors of metabolism are individually rare.
Reason: Collectively they account for about 20% of diagnoses in sick full-term infants.
questions.why: Both true, but their collective frequency in sick infants does not explain that each one is rare.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Newborn screening is performed on a heel-prick blood sample.
Reason: Early treatment of many inborn errors improves the outcome.
questions.why: Both true, but the benefit of early treatment does not explain the sampling method.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Galactosaemia can present with neonatal jaundice.
Reason: Classic galactosaemia is due to galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase deficiency.
questions.why: Both true, but naming the enzyme does not by itself explain the jaundice.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Alkaptonuria causes the urine to darken on standing.
Reason: It is caused by a deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase.
questions.why: Urine does darken, but alkaptonuria is due to homogentisate oxidase deficiency, not PAH.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Pompe disease is a glycogen storage disease.
Reason: It characteristically causes fasting hypoglycaemia.
questions.why: Pompe is a (lysosomal) glycogen storage disease, but it does NOT cause hypoglycaemia.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Homocystinuria causes downward dislocation of the lens.
Reason: It results from a deficiency of homogentisate oxidase.
questions.why: The lens dislocation is correct, but the enzyme defect is cystathionine β-synthase, not homogentisate oxidase.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Hereditary fructose intolerance is caused by fructokinase deficiency.
Reason: Accumulated fructose-1-phosphate inhibits glycogenolysis and causes hypoglycaemia.
questions.why: HFI is due to aldolase B deficiency (assertion false); the fructose-1-phosphate mechanism is correct.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Methylmalonic acidaemia responds to supplementation with biotin.
Reason: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase uses adenosylcobalamin (vitamin B12) as its cofactor.
questions.why: The relevant vitamin is B12, not biotin (assertion false); the cofactor statement is true.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency is inherited as an autosomal recessive trait.
Reason: It is the commonest of the urea cycle defects.
questions.why: OTC deficiency is X-linked (assertion false); it is indeed the commonest urea cycle defect.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Classic galactosaemia is treated with a high-galactose diet.
Reason: Galactose is an essential nutrient that these patients cannot make for themselves.
questions.why: Treatment is a galactose-FREE diet and galactose is not essential; both statements are false.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Phenylketonuria is diagnosed by a positive black-urine test.
Reason: Homogentisic acid accumulates in the urine in phenylketonuria.
questions.why: PKU gives a blue-green ferric chloride test (not black urine), and homogentisic acid is the alkaptonuria metabolite; both false.

questions.stem:
Assertion: MCAD deficiency causes a ketotic hyperglycaemia during fasting.
Reason: Medium-chain fats are the body's main fasting fuel and are over-oxidised in this disorder.
questions.why: MCAD deficiency causes hypoketotic HYPOglycaemia and impaired (not increased) fat oxidation; both false.

questions.stem:
A block in an inborn error of metabolism may produce:
I. Deficiency of an essential product
II. Build-up of a toxic intermediate
III. Formation of a toxic side-product
questions.why: All three are recognised consequences of an enzyme block.

questions.stem:
Classic galactosaemia features:
I. Deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase
II. Cataract formation
III. A completely normal clinical picture
questions.why: I and II true; it is a serious illness, so III is false.

questions.stem:
Von Gierke disease (glycogen storage disease type I):
I. Is a lysosomal storage disorder
II. Is due to glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency
III. Causes fasting hypoglycaemia with hepatomegaly
questions.why: II and III true; it is a cytoplasmic enzyme defect, not lysosomal, so I is false.

questions.stem:
Phenylketonuria:
I. Results from phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency
II. Causes black discolouration of the urine
III. Is managed with a low-phenylalanine diet
questions.why: I and III true; black urine is alkaptonuria, so II is false.

questions.stem:
Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency:
I. Raises urinary orotic acid
II. Is autosomal recessive
III. Lowers the blood ammonia
questions.why: Only I is true; it is X-linked and raises ammonia.

questions.stem:
Urea cycle defects characteristically show:
I. Hyperammonaemia
II. A respiratory alkalosis
III. A low blood urea
questions.why: All three are typical of urea cycle defects.

questions.stem:
Homocystinuria:
I. Is due to cystathionine β-synthase deficiency
II. Causes lens dislocation and thromboembolism
III. Is treated with a high-methionine diet
questions.why: I and II true; the diet is LOW in methionine, so III is false.

questions.stem:
Maple syrup urine disease:
I. Is a disorder of the aromatic amino acids
II. Is due to branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency
III. Produces branched-chain keto acids in the urine
questions.why: II and III true; it involves the BRANCHED-chain (not aromatic) amino acids, so I is false.

questions.stem:
The organic acidaemias (propionic, isovaleric, methylmalonic):
I. Cause a high anion-gap metabolic acidosis
II. Characteristically raise the blood glucose
III. Are diagnosed by urine organic acid analysis
questions.why: I and III true; they do not characteristically raise glucose, so II is false.

questions.stem:
Hereditary fructose intolerance:
I. Is caused by aldolase B deficiency
II. Is treated by increasing dietary fructose
III. Causes hyperglycaemia after fructose
questions.why: Only I is true; treatment is fructose WITHDRAWAL and it causes HYPOglycaemia.

questions.stem:
Fatty acid oxidation disorders typically:
I. Present with fasting hypoketotic hypoglycaemia
II. Are detected by newborn acylcarnitine screening
III. Are worsened by prolonged fasting
questions.why: All three are characteristic of the fatty acid oxidation disorders.

questions.stem:
Albinism:
I. Is due to homogentisate oxidase deficiency
II. Results from a defect in tyrosinase
III. Causes photophobia and nystagmus
questions.why: II and III true; it is a TYROSINASE defect, not homogentisate oxidase, so I is false.

questions.stem: All of the following are inborn errors of CARBOHYDRATE metabolism EXCEPT:
questions.why: Phenylketonuria is an amino-acid disorder, not a carbohydrate one.

questions.stem: All of the following are features of classic galactosaemia EXCEPT:
questions.why: The maple-syrup odour belongs to MSUD, not galactosaemia.

questions.stem: All of the following are urea cycle defects EXCEPT:
questions.why: Isovaleric acidaemia is an organic acidaemia, not a urea cycle defect.

questions.stem: All of the following should raise suspicion of an inborn error in a neonate EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: a family history of neonatal death

options.label: B
options.text: an infant who stays entirely well for weeks

questions.why: IEM typically presents with early deterioration, not prolonged wellbeing.

questions.stem: All of the following are true of MCAD deficiency EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: it is detected on newborn screening

options.label: D
options.text: it is the commonest fatty acid oxidation disorder

questions.why: Cardiomyopathy is a feature of VLCAD and carnitine transporter defects, not MCAD.

questions.stem: All of the following are criteria for neonatal screening of a disease EXCEPT:

options.label: B
options.text: the test should be simple and reliable

options.label: D
options.text: it should be clinically obvious at birth

questions.why: A screenable disease should NOT be clinically apparent at the time of screening.

questions.stem: Classic galactosaemia is caused by deficiency of:
questions.why: Classic galactosaemia is GAL-1-P uridyl transferase deficiency.

questions.stem: The cataract of galactosaemia is caused by lens accumulation of:
questions.why: Aldose reductase converts galactose to galactitol, which osmotically damages the lens.

questions.stem: Hereditary fructose intolerance results from a deficiency of:
questions.why: HFI is aldolase B deficiency, so fructose-1-phosphate accumulates.

questions.stem: The enzyme deficient in Von Gierke disease (GSD type I) is:
questions.why: Von Gierke disease is glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency.

questions.stem: Pompe disease (GSD type II) is a lysosomal deficiency of:
questions.why: Pompe disease is deficiency of lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase.

questions.stem: The enzyme deficient in alkaptonuria is:
questions.why: Alkaptonuria is homogentisate oxidase deficiency; homogentisic acid darkens the urine.

questions.stem: Homocystinuria is most often caused by a deficiency of:
questions.why: Classic homocystinuria is cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency.

questions.stem: The vitamin cofactor required by methylmalonyl-CoA mutase is:
questions.why: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase uses adenosylcobalamin (vitamin B12).

questions.stem: The X-linked urea cycle defect that raises urinary orotic acid is:
questions.why: OTC deficiency is X-linked and diverts carbamoyl phosphate to orotic acid.

questions.stem: The commonest fatty acid oxidation disorder is:
questions.why: MCAD deficiency is the most common fatty acid oxidation disorder.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Carbon tetrachloride causes liver cell damage.
Reason: It is metabolised to the trichloromethyl radical, which initiates lipid peroxidation.
questions.why: The trichloromethyl radical triggering lipid peroxidation is exactly how CCl4 injures hepatocytes.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Glutathione peroxidase activity depends on an adequate dietary intake of selenium.
Reason: Glutathione peroxidase is a selenium-containing enzyme (a selenoprotein).
questions.why: Because it is a selenoprotein, selenium supply directly limits its activity.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Reactive oxygen species can increase HIV replication.
Reason: Oxidative stress activates the transcription factor NF-κB.
questions.why: NF-κB activation driving viral gene expression is the mechanism linking ROS to HIV replication.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Allopurinol can reduce ischaemia-reperfusion injury.
Reason: It inhibits xanthine oxidase, a source of superoxide generated on reperfusion.
questions.why: Blocking xanthine oxidase removes the superoxide burst, which is how allopurinol protects.

questions.stem:
Assertion: The mitochondrial isoenzyme of superoxide dismutase contains manganese.
Reason: The cytosolic isoenzyme of superoxide dismutase contains copper and zinc.
questions.why: Both are true, but the cytosolic cofactors do not explain the manganese in the mitochondrial form.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Ceruloplasmin has antioxidant activity in plasma.
Reason: Haptoglobin binds free haemoglobin released into the plasma.
questions.why: Both are true plasma antioxidant facts, but haptoglobin's role does not explain ceruloplasmin's.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Flavonoids in green tea and berries have antioxidant properties.
Reason: Carotenoids are found in carrots, tomatoes and spinach.
questions.why: Both are true dietary-antioxidant facts, but one does not explain the other.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Transferrin and lactoferrin act as antioxidants.
Reason: They work by generating hydrogen peroxide that destroys radicals.
questions.why: They are antioxidants, but they act by SEQUESTERING iron, not by making hydrogen peroxide.

questions.stem:
Assertion: The trichloromethyl radical is derived from carbon tetrachloride.
Reason: Carbon tetrachloride is an endogenous metabolite formed from glycine.
questions.why: The radical does come from CCl4, but CCl4 is an exogenous solvent, not a glycine metabolite.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Allopurinol is regarded as an antioxidant drug.
Reason: It works by directly scavenging the hydroxyl radical within membranes.
questions.why: It is antioxidant, but it acts by inhibiting xanthine oxidase, not by scavenging hydroxyl radicals.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Glutathione peroxidase requires copper as its cofactor.
Reason: Dietary selenium deficiency impairs antioxidant defence.
questions.why: Glutathione peroxidase uses selenium, not copper (assertion false); selenium lack does impair defence (reason true).

questions.stem:
Assertion: The termination step of lipid peroxidation generates fresh peroxyl radicals.
Reason: During propagation, a carbon radical reacts with oxygen to form a peroxyl radical.
questions.why: Termination combines radicals into NON-radical products (assertion false); the propagation statement is true.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Desferrioxamine acts by directly scavenging singlet oxygen.
Reason: Desferrioxamine chelates iron and blocks metal-catalysed radical formation.
questions.why: Desferrioxamine works by iron chelation, not singlet-oxygen scavenging (assertion false); the reason is true.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Lipid peroxidation consists only of initiation and propagation, with no termination step.
Reason: Peroxyl radicals are unable to react with one another.
questions.why: There is a termination step and peroxyl radicals do combine; both statements are false.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Oxygen toxicity refers to the beneficial effect of oxygen on cells.
Reason: Reactive oxygen species are never harmful to tissues.
questions.why: Oxygen toxicity is the harmful effect of oxidative species, which clearly do damage tissue; both false.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Uric acid is purely a pro-oxidant with no protective role.
Reason: Humans synthesise large amounts of vitamin C as their main antioxidant.
questions.why: Urate is actually an antioxidant, and humans cannot synthesise vitamin C; both statements are false.

questions.stem:
Recognised free-radical species include:
I. the trichloromethyl radical (CCl3•)
II. the thiyl radical (RS•)
III. the alkoxyl radical (RO•)
questions.why: All three are carbon-, sulphur- and oxygen-centred free radicals.

questions.stem:
Mechanisms of free-radical cell injury include:
I. covalent binding of xenobiotics
II. disturbance of calcium homeostasis
III. direct synthesis of ATP
questions.why: I and II are true; ATP synthesis is not a mechanism of radical injury, so III is false.

questions.stem:
Concerning the superoxide dismutase isoenzymes:
I. the mitochondrial form uses selenium
II. the mitochondrial form uses manganese
III. the cytosolic form uses copper and zinc
questions.why: II and III are true; the mitochondrial enzyme uses manganese, not selenium, so I is false.

questions.stem:
Metal-binding (preventive) antioxidant proteins include:
I. transferrin
II. glutathione peroxidase
III. ceruloplasmin
questions.why: I and III are metal-binding proteins; glutathione peroxidase is a catalytic (scavenging) enzyme, so II is false.

questions.stem:
The trichloromethyl radical:
I. is formed from carbon tetrachloride
II. is a normal product of respiration
III. is itself an antioxidant enzyme
questions.why: Only I is true; it is a xenobiotic-derived radical, not a respiratory product or an enzyme.

questions.stem:
Reactive oxygen species can act as signalling molecules by:
I. activating the NF-κB pathway
II. influencing inflammation and apoptosis genes
III. having roles at low physiological concentrations
questions.why: All three reflect the recognised signalling role of ROS.

questions.stem:
Endogenous enzymatic sources of free radicals include:
I. xanthine oxidase
II. prostaglandin synthase (cyclo-oxygenase)
III. superoxide dismutase
questions.why: I and II generate radicals; superoxide dismutase REMOVES superoxide, so III is false.

questions.stem:
In HIV infection:
I. patients have raised glutathione levels
II. hydrogen peroxide can promote viral gene expression
III. oxidative stress activates NF-κB and raises viral replication
questions.why: II and III are true; glutathione is LOWER in HIV patients, so I is false.

questions.stem:
Factors that increase free-radical production include:
I. cigarette smoke
II. a diet rich in antioxidants
III. ionising radiation
questions.why: I and III raise radical load; a diet rich in antioxidants lowers it, so II is false.

questions.stem:
Glutathione peroxidase:
I. is a selenium-containing enzyme
II. requires copper for its activity
III. is an extracellular metal-binding protein
questions.why: Only I is true; it is a selenoprotein, an intracellular catalytic enzyme, not copper-dependent.

questions.stem:
Non-enzymatic antioxidants include:
I. urate (uric acid)
II. coenzyme Q10
III. alpha-lipoic acid
questions.why: All three are recognised non-enzymatic antioxidants.

questions.stem:
Regarding lipid peroxidation:
I. it needs no termination step
II. it is initiated by hydrogen abstraction from a polyunsaturated fatty acid
III. it yields malondialdehyde, which forms DNA adducts
questions.why: II and III are true; peroxidation does have a termination step, so I is false.

questions.stem: All of the following are free radicals EXCEPT:
questions.why: Hydrogen peroxide has no unpaired electron; it is a non-radical reactive oxygen species.

questions.stem: All of the following are mechanisms of free-radical toxicity EXCEPT:
questions.why: ATP synthesis is normal energy metabolism, not a mechanism of radical injury.

questions.stem: All of the following drugs or chemicals generate free radicals EXCEPT:
questions.why: Desferrioxamine is an iron-chelating ANTIoxidant; the others are radical generators.

questions.stem: All of the following are metal-binding antioxidant proteins EXCEPT:
questions.why: Catalase is a haem enzyme that destroys hydrogen peroxide, not a metal-sequestering protein.

questions.stem: All of the following increase free-radical production EXCEPT:
questions.why: Dietary flavonoids are antioxidants and reduce, rather than raise, radical load.

questions.stem: All of the following are recognised modes of antioxidant action EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: reducing the concentration of reactive species

options.label: D
options.text: generating superoxide to drive the Fenton reaction

questions.why: Generating superoxide is pro-oxidant; antioxidants do the opposite.

questions.stem: Oxygen toxicity is best defined as the:

options.label: A
options.text: beneficial role of oxygen in metabolism

options.label: B
options.text: inability of a cell to take up oxygen

options.label: C
options.text: deficiency of oxygen supply to a tissue

options.label: D
options.text: storage of oxygen by muscle myoglobin

options.label: E
options.text: toxic effect of oxidative radicals on cells

questions.why: Oxygen toxicity is the harmful effect of oxidative radical species at the cellular level.

questions.stem: The stepwise four-electron reduction of oxygen to water produces, as intermediates:

options.label: A
options.text: superoxide, peroxide and the hydroxyl radical

options.label: E
options.text: hydrogen peroxide as the sole product

questions.why: Adding electrons to O2 one at a time yields superoxide, then hydrogen peroxide, then the hydroxyl radical.

questions.stem: Carbon tetrachloride is converted in the liver into the damaging:
questions.why: Hepatic metabolism of CCl4 forms the trichloromethyl radical, initiating lipid peroxidation.

questions.stem: The mitochondrial isoenzyme of superoxide dismutase contains:
questions.why: Mitochondrial SOD is the manganese enzyme (MnSOD); the cytosolic form uses copper and zinc.

questions.stem: Because glutathione peroxidase is a selenoprotein, its activity depends on dietary:
questions.why: Glutathione peroxidase needs selenium at its active site.

questions.stem: The plasma copper-binding protein with antioxidant (ferroxidase) activity is:
questions.why: Ceruloplasmin binds copper and, as a ferroxidase, limits iron-driven radical formation.

questions.stem: The plasma protein that binds free haemoglobin released during haemolysis is:
questions.why: Haptoglobin mops up free haemoglobin, limiting its pro-oxidant iron.

questions.stem: The termination step of lipid peroxidation occurs when:

options.label: B
options.text: two radicals combine to give a non-radical product

options.label: C
options.text: a radical abstracts hydrogen from a fatty acid

options.label: D
options.text: a carbon radical reacts with molecular oxygen

options.label: E
options.text: a peroxyl radical attacks a new fatty acid

questions.why: Termination is two radicals joining to form a stable non-radical product, ending the chain.

questions.stem: The iron-chelating antioxidant drug that blocks metal-catalysed radical formation is:
questions.why: Desferrioxamine chelates iron, preventing the Fenton reaction.

questions.stem: Reactive oxygen species influence gene expression largely through the transcription factor:
questions.why: ROS activate NF-κB, which regulates immunity, inflammation and apoptosis genes.

questions.stem: The end-product of lipid peroxidation that forms mutagenic DNA adducts is:
questions.why: Malondialdehyde (MDA) reacts with DNA bases to form mutagenic adducts.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Congenital erythropoietic porphyria causes severe cutaneous photosensitivity.
Reason: Uroporphyrinogen III synthase deficiency lets phototoxic uroporphyrin I accumulate in the skin.
questions.why: The build-up of phototoxic porphyrin is exactly why the skin is so light-sensitive.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Variegate porphyria is especially common in white South Africans.
Reason: It is autosomal dominant and traceable to a common founder in that population.
questions.why: A founder effect in an autosomal dominant disorder explains the high local frequency.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Crigler-Najjar syndrome type II responds to phenobarbital.
Reason: Phenobarbital induces the residual UDP-glucuronyl transferase activity.
questions.why: Enzyme induction raising the partial UGT activity is why phenobarbital helps type II.

questions.stem:
Assertion: In obstructive jaundice the urine becomes dark.
Reason: Water-soluble conjugated bilirubin is filtered and excreted in the urine.
questions.why: Conjugated bilirubin spilling into urine is exactly what darkens it in obstruction.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Erythropoietic protoporphyria causes photosensitivity.
Reason: Acute intermittent porphyria is not photosensitive.
questions.why: Both statements are true but concern different porphyrias, so one does not explain the other.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Ferrochelatase is a mitochondrial enzyme.
Reason: ALA dehydratase is a cytosolic enzyme.
questions.why: Both compartment facts are true, but one does not explain the other.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Conjugated bilirubin gives a direct van den Bergh reaction.
Reason: It must first be exposed to methanol before it will react with the diazo reagent.
questions.why: Conjugated bilirubin reacts directly WITHOUT alcohol; it is the unconjugated fraction that needs methanol.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Dubin-Johnson syndrome produces a conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia.
Reason: It is caused by a deficiency of UDP-glucuronyl transferase.
questions.why: The conjugated picture is right, but the defect is in canalicular excretion (MRP2), not conjugation.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Hereditary coproporphyria can cause acute neurovisceral attacks.
Reason: It results from a deficiency of ferrochelatase.
questions.why: Acute attacks do occur, but the deficient enzyme is coproporphyrinogen oxidase, not ferrochelatase.

questions.stem:
Assertion: In haemolytic (prehepatic) jaundice bilirubin appears in the urine.
Reason: Unconjugated bilirubin is tightly bound to albumin and is not filtered by the kidney.
questions.why: There is NO bilirubinuria in haemolysis (assertion false); the albumin-binding reason is true.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Biliverdin reductase uses FAD as its source of reducing power.
Reason: NADPH supplies the electrons for the conversion of biliverdin to bilirubin.
questions.why: The reductant is NADPH, not FAD (assertion false); the NADPH statement is true.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Gilbert syndrome causes a conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with dark urine.
Reason: It is due to a complete absence of UDP-glucuronyl transferase.
questions.why: Gilbert's is a mild UNconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with only partial UGT reduction; both statements are false.

questions.stem:
Enzymes located in the mitochondrion during haem synthesis include:
I. ALA synthase
II. Coproporphyrinogen oxidase
III. Ferrochelatase
questions.why: All three act in the mitochondrion; the middle steps are cytosolic.

questions.stem:
Features of an acute porphyric attack include:
I. Abdominal pain
II. Neuropsychiatric disturbance
III. Relief by continued fasting
questions.why: I and II are typical; fasting precipitates (not relieves) attacks, so III is false.

questions.stem:
Congenital erythropoietic porphyria:
I. Is an acute hepatic porphyria with no skin signs
II. Causes severe cutaneous photosensitivity
III. Can stain the teeth red-brown (erythrodontia)
questions.why: II and III are true; it is an erythropoietic, photosensitive disorder, so I is false.

questions.stem:
In complete biliary obstruction:
I. Plasma conjugated bilirubin is raised
II. Urinary urobilinogen is increased
III. The stools become pale
questions.why: I and III are true; urobilinogen is absent because bile cannot reach the gut, so II is false.

questions.stem:
Gilbert syndrome:
I. Causes a mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia
II. Commonly leads to kernicterus in adults
III. Requires lifelong phototherapy
questions.why: Only I is true; it is benign, needing no phototherapy and not causing kernicterus.

questions.stem:
Recognised precipitants of an acute porphyria attack include:
I. Drugs that induce cytochrome P450
II. Prolonged fasting
III. Alcohol
questions.why: All three raise ALA-synthase demand and can trigger an attack.

questions.stem:
Lead poisoning characteristically causes:
I. Inhibition of ferrochelatase
II. Basophilic stippling of red cells
III. A markedly raised blood haem level
questions.why: I and II are true; haem synthesis falls (not rises) in lead poisoning, so III is false.

questions.stem:
Crigler-Najjar syndrome type I:
I. Responds well to phenobarbital
II. Results from total absence of UDP-glucuronyl transferase
III. Causes severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and kernicterus
questions.why: II and III are true; type I has no enzyme to induce, so it does not respond to phenobarbital.

questions.stem:
Haem-containing proteins with enzymatic roles include:
I. Catalase
II. Carbonic anhydrase
III. Cytochrome P450
questions.why: I and III are haem enzymes; carbonic anhydrase is a zinc enzyme, so II is false.

questions.stem:
Erythropoietic protoporphyria:
I. Is caused by ferrochelatase deficiency
II. Causes dark urine with neurovisceral attacks
III. Is the commonest acute porphyria
questions.why: Only I is true; it is a photosensitive (not acute neurovisceral) porphyria.

questions.stem:
The van den Bergh reaction:
I. Measures bilirubin using a diazo reagent
II. Its direct fraction corresponds to conjugated bilirubin
III. Its indirect fraction corresponds to unconjugated bilirubin
questions.why: All three correctly describe the van den Bergh test.

questions.stem:
Steps of haem synthesis that occur in the cytosol include:
I. Insertion of iron by ferrochelatase
II. Formation of porphobilinogen by ALA dehydratase
III. Formation of hydroxymethylbilane by PBG deaminase
questions.why: II and III are cytosolic; ferrochelatase is mitochondrial, so I is false.

questions.stem: All of the following porphyrias are photosensitive EXCEPT:
questions.why: Acute intermittent porphyria is purely neurovisceral, with no photosensitivity.

questions.stem: All of the following are enzymes of haem synthesis EXCEPT:
questions.why: Biliverdin reductase is part of haem CATABOLISM, not synthesis.

questions.stem: All of the following occur in obstructive (post-hepatic) jaundice EXCEPT:
questions.why: With bile flow blocked, no bilirubin reaches the gut, so urobilinogen falls.

questions.stem: All of the following cause a predominantly CONJUGATED hyperbilirubinaemia EXCEPT:
questions.why: Crigler-Najjar is a defect of conjugation, so its hyperbilirubinaemia is unconjugated.

questions.stem: All of the following precipitate an acute porphyria attack EXCEPT:
questions.why: Glucose loading suppresses ALA synthase and relieves attacks.

questions.stem: All of the following are true of lead poisoning EXCEPT:
questions.why: Lead impairs haem synthesis and causes anaemia, so haemoglobin falls.

questions.stem: The enzyme that condenses two molecules of ALA into porphobilinogen is:
questions.why: ALA dehydratase (PBG synthase) joins two ALA to form porphobilinogen.

questions.stem: Ring closure to form uroporphyrinogen III is catalysed by:
questions.why: Uroporphyrinogen III synthase closes and flips the ring to give the III isomer.

questions.stem: The haem-synthesis enzyme deficient in variegate porphyria is:
questions.why: Variegate porphyria is protoporphyrinogen oxidase deficiency.

questions.stem: The enzyme deficient in hereditary coproporphyria is:
questions.why: Hereditary coproporphyria is coproporphyrinogen oxidase deficiency.

questions.stem: The enzyme deficient in congenital erythropoietic porphyria is:
questions.why: CEP is uroporphyrinogen III synthase deficiency.

questions.stem: The enzyme deficient in erythropoietic protoporphyria is:
questions.why: Erythropoietic protoporphyria is ferrochelatase deficiency.

questions.stem: The erythroid form of ALA synthase (ALAS2) is regulated mainly by cellular:
questions.why: ALAS2 is controlled by iron through an iron-responsive element.

questions.stem: A loss-of-function mutation in erythroid ALA synthase (ALAS2) causes:
questions.why: ALAS2 deficiency impairs erythroid haem synthesis, giving X-linked sideroblastic anaemia.

questions.stem: Biliverdin is reduced to bilirubin by biliverdin reductase using:
questions.why: Biliverdin reductase uses NADPH as the reductant.

questions.stem: In the van den Bergh reaction, the direct-reacting fraction corresponds to:
questions.why: The direct fraction is conjugated (water-soluble) bilirubin.

questions.stem: The transporter that is defective in Dubin-Johnson syndrome is:
questions.why: Dubin-Johnson is a defect of the canalicular MRP2 export pump for conjugated bilirubin.

questions.stem: Crigler-Najjar syndrome type I is characterised by:

options.label: A
options.text: an excessive rate of red-cell haemolysis

options.label: C
options.text: a mildly reduced level of the transferase

options.label: E
options.text: a defect of hepatic bilirubin uptake

questions.why: Type I has no UGT activity, giving severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and kernicterus.

questions.stem: In haemolytic (prehepatic) jaundice, the urine typically shows:
questions.why: Excess unconjugated bilirubin is not filtered, but extra urobilinogen reaches the urine.

questions.stem: Pale clay-coloured stools with dark urine are most typical of:
questions.why: Blocked bile flow gives pale stools and dark (conjugated bilirubin) urine.

questions.stem: The pigment that gives the faeces their normal brown colour is:
questions.why: Stercobilin, formed from urobilinogen in the gut, colours the faeces.

questions.stem: Blue-light phototherapy for neonatal jaundice works by:
questions.why: Light isomerises bilirubin to water-soluble forms excreted without conjugation.

questions.stem: Coarse basophilic stippling of red cells is characteristically seen in:
questions.why: Lead inhibits pyrimidine 5'-nucleotidase, leaving stippled ribosomal remnants.

questions.stem: A severe acute intermittent porphyria attack is best treated with intravenous:
questions.why: Haem arginate replenishes the haem pool and feedback-inhibits ALA synthase.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Red cells sickle in sickle-cell disease when the oxygen tension falls.
Reason: Deoxygenated haemoglobin S polymerises into rigid fibres that distort the cell.
questions.why: HbS polymerisation on deoxygenation is exactly what deforms the cell into a sickle.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Sickle-cell trait gives some protection against falciparum malaria.
Reason: Parasitised trait cells tend to sickle and are removed, limiting parasite growth.
questions.why: Preferential sickling and clearance of infected cells is the basis of malaria protection.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Methaemoglobinaemia produces cyanosis that does not improve with oxygen.
Reason: Ferric (Fe3+) methaemoglobin is unable to bind oxygen.
questions.why: Because the ferric haem cannot carry O2, giving oxygen does not relieve the cyanosis.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Hydroxyurea reduces the frequency of sickle-cell crises.
Reason: It raises fetal haemoglobin (HbF), which interferes with HbS polymerisation.
questions.why: Raising HbF to block HbS polymerisation is how hydroxyurea works.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Carbon monoxide poisoning shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the left.
Reason: Haemoglobin A is a tetramer of two alpha and two beta chains.
questions.why: Both are true, but the subunit composition does not explain the curve shift.

questions.stem:
Assertion: HbA1c reflects average blood glucose over the preceding weeks.
Reason: Methaemoglobin contains iron in the ferric state.
questions.why: Both statements are true but unrelated, so one cannot explain the other.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Sickle-cell disease arises from a single amino-acid substitution in the beta chain.
Reason: Valine at position 6 is replaced by glutamate.
questions.why: A single substitution is right, but it is glutamate that is replaced BY valine, so the reason is reversed.

questions.stem:
Assertion: In carbon monoxide poisoning the blood and skin look cherry-red.
Reason: Carboxyhaemoglobin binds carbon monoxide far more weakly than it binds oxygen.
questions.why: The cherry-red colour is real, but CO binds about 200 times more tightly than O2, so the reason is false.

questions.stem:
Assertion: The Haldane effect is the enhanced carriage of CO2 by deoxygenated haemoglobin.
Reason: Oxygenation of haemoglobin increases its ability to bind CO2 and protons.
questions.why: The Haldane effect is correctly defined, but oxygenation DECREASES CO2/H+ binding, so the reason is false.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Most carbon dioxide is carried in blood bound directly to the haem iron.
Reason: The bulk of CO2 is transported as bicarbonate generated by carbonic anhydrase.
questions.why: CO2 is not carried on the haem iron (assertion false); the bicarbonate statement is true.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Acquired methaemoglobinaemia is treated with intravenous iron.
Reason: Methylene blue reduces methaemoglobin back to functional haemoglobin.
questions.why: The treatment is methylene blue, not iron (assertion false); the methylene-blue reason is true.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Fetal haemoglobin remains the major haemoglobin throughout the first years of life.
Reason: Fetal haemoglobin has the chain composition alpha-2 gamma-2.
questions.why: HbF is largely replaced by HbA within months of birth (assertion false); the composition is correct.

questions.stem:
Assertion: HbA1c is produced by enzymatic phosphorylation of haemoglobin.
Reason: It measures the blood glucose at the exact moment of sampling.
questions.why: HbA1c forms by NON-enzymatic glycation and reflects weeks of glycaemia, not the instant; both false.

questions.stem:
Assertion: The chloride (Hamburger) shift is chloride leaving the red cell as bicarbonate enters.
Reason: Carbonic anhydrase is absent from red blood cells.
questions.why: The shift is chloride entering as bicarbonate leaves, and red cells are rich in carbonic anhydrase; both false.

questions.stem:
Features of sickle-cell disease include:
I. a glutamate-to-valine change at position 6 of the beta chain
II. polymerisation of HbS when deoxygenated
III. vaso-occlusive painful crises
questions.why: All three are core features of sickle-cell disease.

questions.stem:
Methaemoglobinaemia:
I. contains iron in the ferric (Fe3+) state
II. causes cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen
III. has a higher oxygen-carrying capacity than normal blood
questions.why: I and II are true; methaemoglobin cannot carry oxygen, so III is false.

questions.stem:
The Bohr and Haldane effects:
I. are abolished in the normal adult
II. mean deoxyhaemoglobin binds more CO2 and H+
III. help unload oxygen in tissues and load it in the lungs
questions.why: II and III are true; the effects are normal physiology, so I is false.

questions.stem:
Carbon dioxide is transported in the blood:
I. mostly as bicarbonate
II. mostly bound to the haem iron
III. partly as carbamino-haemoglobin
questions.why: I and III are true; CO2 binds the globin amino groups, not the haem iron, so II is false.

questions.stem:
Carbon monoxide poisoning:
I. forms carboxyhaemoglobin
II. shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the right
III. lowers haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen
questions.why: Only I is true; CO shifts the curve LEFT and raises O2 affinity of remaining sites.

questions.stem:
Hydroxyurea in sickle-cell disease:
I. raises the level of fetal haemoglobin
II. reduces the frequency of painful crises
III. interferes with HbS polymerisation
questions.why: All three describe how hydroxyurea helps.

questions.stem:
Causes of ACQUIRED methaemoglobinaemia include:
I. nitrites
II. dapsone
III. an inherited deficiency of cytochrome b5 reductase
questions.why: I and II are acquired causes; the enzyme deficiency is congenital, so III is false.

questions.stem:
Haemoglobin A1c:
I. is formed by an enzyme-catalysed reaction
II. forms by non-enzymatic glycation of the beta chain
III. reflects average glucose over the preceding weeks
questions.why: II and III are true; glycation is non-enzymatic, so I is false.

questions.stem:
The chloride (Hamburger) shift:
I. moves chloride into the red cell as bicarbonate leaves
II. occurs without any carbonic anhydrase
III. helps the blood to carry carbon dioxide
questions.why: I and III are true; it depends on carbonic anhydrase, so II is false.

questions.stem:
Fetal haemoglobin (HbF):
I. has the composition alpha-2 gamma-2
II. remains the main haemoglobin throughout childhood
III. binds 2,3-BPG more avidly than HbA
questions.why: Only I is true; HbF is replaced within months and binds BPG weakly.

questions.stem:
The oxygen dissociation curve shifts to the RIGHT with:
I. a rise in temperature
II. a rise in 2,3-BPG
III. a fall in pH
questions.why: All three lower oxygen affinity and shift the curve right.

questions.stem:
In sickle-cell TRAIT:
I. more than half of the haemoglobin is HbS
II. the person is usually asymptomatic
III. there is relative protection against malaria
questions.why: II and III are true; in trait HbA predominates (HbS <50%), so I is false.

questions.stem: All of the following are true of sickle-cell disease EXCEPT:

options.label: B
options.text: it is caused by a defect in the alpha-globin gene

options.label: D
options.text: there is a glutamate-to-valine change at beta-6

questions.why: Sickle-cell disease is a beta-globin defect, not an alpha-globin one.

questions.stem: All of the following cause ACQUIRED methaemoglobinaemia EXCEPT:
questions.why: Cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency is a congenital, not acquired, cause.

questions.stem: All of the following are ways CO2 is carried in blood EXCEPT:
questions.why: CO2 binds globin amino groups (carbamino), not the haem iron, which carries O2.

questions.stem: All of the following shift the oxygen dissociation curve to the RIGHT EXCEPT:
questions.why: Carbon monoxide shifts the curve to the LEFT, worsening oxygen delivery.

questions.stem: All of the following are true of HbA1c EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: it is formed by an enzymatic reaction

options.label: C
options.text: it forms by glycation of the beta chain

options.label: D
options.text: it rises in poorly controlled diabetes

questions.why: HbA1c forms by NON-enzymatic glycation, not an enzyme reaction.

questions.stem: All of the following are normal (physiological) haemoglobins EXCEPT:
questions.why: Haemoglobin S is an abnormal variant, not a normal physiological haemoglobin.

questions.stem: In sickle-cell disease, the glutamate at position 6 of the beta chain is replaced by:
questions.why: HbS has valine substituted for glutamate at beta-6.

questions.stem: Haemoglobin C arises from substitution at beta-6 of glutamate by:
questions.why: HbC has lysine in place of glutamate at beta-6.

questions.stem: Haemoglobin S polymerises and sickles the red cell when it is:
questions.why: Deoxy-HbS polymerises into fibres that sickle the cell.

questions.stem: The definitive test to identify and quantify abnormal haemoglobins is:
questions.why: Electrophoresis separates and quantifies the haemoglobin variants.

questions.stem: Hydroxyurea helps sickle-cell patients chiefly by raising:
questions.why: Raised HbF dilutes HbS and blocks its polymerisation.

questions.stem: In methaemoglobinaemia the haem iron is in the:
questions.why: Methaemoglobin has oxidised ferric (Fe3+) iron that cannot bind O2.

questions.stem: The enzyme deficient in congenital methaemoglobinaemia is:
questions.why: Congenital methaemoglobinaemia is cytochrome b5 (methaemoglobin) reductase deficiency.

questions.stem: Acquired methaemoglobinaemia is treated with:
questions.why: Methylene blue reduces methaemoglobin back to functional haemoglobin.

questions.stem: In carbon monoxide poisoning the blood is classically:
questions.why: Carboxyhaemoglobin gives the blood and skin a cherry-red colour.

questions.stem: Besides blocking oxygen binding, carbon monoxide is harmful because it:

options.label: B
options.text: shifts the oxygen curve to the left

options.label: C
options.text: shifts the oxygen curve to the right

options.label: D
options.text: has no effect on the curve

questions.why: CO shifts the curve left, so the remaining oxygen is released less readily to tissues.

questions.stem: Most carbon dioxide is transported in the blood as:
questions.why: About 70% of CO2 travels as bicarbonate.

questions.stem: The red-cell enzyme that hydrates CO2 to carbonic acid is:
questions.why: Carbonic anhydrase rapidly converts CO2 and water to carbonic acid.

questions.stem: The Haldane effect states that:

options.label: B
options.text: CO2 has no effect on oxygen binding

options.label: C
options.text: a low pH raises oxygen affinity

questions.why: Deoxyhaemoglobin binds CO2 and H+ more readily - the Haldane effect.

questions.stem: The chloride (Hamburger) shift involves movement of chloride:

options.label: A
options.text: into the red cell as bicarbonate leaves

options.label: B
options.text: out of the red cell as bicarbonate enters

options.label: C
options.text: into the plasma together with sodium

questions.why: Chloride enters the red cell to balance bicarbonate leaving it.

questions.stem: Adult haemoglobin A2 has the chain composition:
questions.why: HbA2 is two alpha and two delta chains.

questions.stem: HbA1c is formed by:
questions.why: Glucose adds non-enzymatically to haemoglobin to form HbA1c.

questions.stem: Massive release of myoglobin into the urine (myoglobinuria) after muscle breakdown can cause:
questions.why: Myoglobin is nephrotoxic and can precipitate acute kidney injury in rhabdomyolysis.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Tay-Sachs disease causes a cherry-red spot at the macula.
Reason: Hexosaminidase A deficiency lets GM2 ganglioside accumulate in retinal ganglion cells.
questions.why: Ganglioside build-up in the retinal ganglion cells is exactly what produces the cherry-red spot.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome causes hyperuricaemia.
Reason: HGPRT deficiency blocks purine salvage, so purines are degraded to uric acid.
questions.why: Loss of salvage diverting purines to uric acid is why urate rises.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Wilson's disease can be treated with penicillamine.
Reason: Penicillamine chelates the copper that accumulates in the tissues.
questions.why: Copper chelation is exactly how penicillamine treats Wilson's disease.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Hurler syndrome is a mucopolysaccharidosis.
Reason: Tay-Sachs disease is a sphingolipidosis.
questions.why: Both classifications are correct but concern different diseases, so one does not explain the other.

questions.stem:
Assertion: McArdle disease causes exercise intolerance.
Reason: Von Gierke disease causes fasting hypoglycaemia.
questions.why: Both are true glycogen-storage facts but about different diseases, so one cannot explain the other.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Hunter syndrome is inherited in an X-linked manner.
Reason: It is caused by a deficiency of alpha-L-iduronidase.
questions.why: Hunter is X-linked, but its enzyme is iduronate-2-sulfatase; alpha-L-iduronidase is Hurler, so the reason is false.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is X-linked.
Reason: It is due to a deficiency of adenosine deaminase.
questions.why: It is X-linked, but the deficient enzyme is HGPRT; adenosine deaminase deficiency causes SCID, so the reason is false.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Wilson's disease is associated with Kayser-Fleischer rings.
Reason: It is caused by excessive intestinal absorption of iron.
questions.why: The rings are correct, but Wilson's is copper (not iron) overload, so the reason is false.

questions.stem:
Assertion: McArdle disease is due to a deficiency of liver glycogen phosphorylase.
Reason: Deficiency of muscle glycogen phosphorylase impairs glycogen breakdown during exercise.
questions.why: McArdle affects MUSCLE phosphorylase (assertion names liver - false); the muscle statement is true.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Fabry disease is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner.
Reason: It results from a deficiency of alpha-galactosidase A.
questions.why: Fabry is X-linked (assertion false); the enzyme named is correct.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Von Gierke disease is a lysosomal storage disorder treated by enzyme replacement.
Reason: Its enzyme, glucose-6-phosphatase, lies within the lysosome.
questions.why: Von Gierke is a cytoplasmic/ER glucose-6-phosphatase defect, not a lysosomal disease; both statements are false.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Essential fructosuria is a serious disease needing urgent treatment.
Reason: It is caused by a deficiency of aldolase B.
questions.why: Essential fructosuria is benign and due to FRUCTOKINASE deficiency (aldolase B is HFI); both false.

questions.stem:
Lysosomal storage diseases include:
I. Tay-Sachs disease
II. Gaucher disease
III. Hurler syndrome
questions.why: All three are lysosomal storage disorders.

questions.stem:
Tay-Sachs disease:
I. is due to hexosaminidase A deficiency
II. causes a cherry-red macular spot
III. causes gross hepatosplenomegaly
questions.why: I and II are true; Tay-Sachs has NO organomegaly, so III is false.

questions.stem:
Lesch-Nyhan syndrome:
I. is autosomal recessive
II. is due to HGPRT deficiency
III. causes hyperuricaemia and self-mutilation
questions.why: II and III are true; it is X-linked, so I is false.

questions.stem:
McArdle disease (glycogen storage disease type V):
I. affects muscle glycogen phosphorylase
II. causes fasting hypoglycaemia
III. presents with exercise intolerance and cramps
questions.why: I and III are true; being a muscle disorder it does not cause hypoglycaemia, so II is false.

questions.stem:
Fabry disease:
I. is due to alpha-galactosidase A deficiency
II. is autosomal recessive
III. causes corneal clouding as its only feature
questions.why: Only I is true; it is X-linked and a multisystem disorder.

questions.stem:
Gaucher disease:
I. is due to glucocerebrosidase deficiency
II. causes hepatosplenomegaly
III. shows lipid-laden Gaucher cells
questions.why: All three are characteristic of Gaucher disease.

questions.stem:
Features distinguishing Hunter from Hurler syndrome include:
I. Hunter is X-linked
II. Hunter lacks corneal clouding
III. Hunter is due to alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency
questions.why: I and II are true; Hunter is iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency, so III is false.

questions.stem:
Wilson's disease:
I. is a disorder of iron overload
II. shows Kayser-Fleischer rings
III. has a low serum ceruloplasmin
questions.why: II and III are true; it is COPPER overload, so I is false.

questions.stem:
Peroxisomal disorders:
I. include Zellweger syndrome
II. are due to lysosomal enzyme defects
III. include X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy with raised very-long-chain fatty acids
questions.why: I and III are true; the defect is peroxisomal, not lysosomal, so II is false.

questions.stem:
Von Gierke disease (glycogen storage disease type I):
I. is due to glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency
II. is a lysosomal storage disease
III. is treated by enzyme replacement therapy
questions.why: Only I is true; it is not lysosomal and is managed with diet, not enzyme replacement.

questions.stem:
Niemann-Pick disease:
I. is due to sphingomyelinase deficiency
II. causes hepatosplenomegaly
III. can show a cherry-red macular spot
questions.why: All three are features of Niemann-Pick disease.

questions.stem:
In Lesch-Nyhan syndrome hyperuricaemia arises because:
I. uric acid production is reduced
II. purine salvage via HGPRT is lost
III. purines are instead degraded to uric acid
questions.why: II and III are true; urate production is increased, so I is false.

questions.why: Von Gierke disease is a glycogen storage disease (glucose-6-phosphatase), not lysosomal.

questions.stem: All of the following are sphingolipidoses EXCEPT:
questions.why: Hurler is a mucopolysaccharidosis, not a sphingolipidosis.

questions.why: Hurler shows corneal clouding, not a cherry-red spot.

questions.stem: All of the following are X-linked EXCEPT:
questions.why: Gaucher disease is autosomal recessive; the others are X-linked.

questions.stem: All of the following are true of Wilson's disease EXCEPT:

options.label: C
options.text: a defect in the ATP7B gene

questions.why: Serum ceruloplasmin is characteristically LOW in Wilson's disease.

questions.why: Tay-Sachs is a lysosomal sphingolipidosis, not a glycogen storage disease.

questions.why: Tay-Sachs is hexosaminidase A deficiency with GM2 accumulation.

questions.why: Loss of hexosaminidase A causes GM2 ganglioside accumulation.

questions.why: Gaucher disease is glucocerebrosidase deficiency.

questions.why: Niemann-Pick disease is sphingomyelinase deficiency.

questions.why: Hunter syndrome characteristically spares the cornea (no clouding).

questions.stem: A deficiency of adenosine deaminase classically causes:
questions.why: Adenosine deaminase deficiency causes severe combined immunodeficiency.

questions.stem: Hereditary orotic aciduria is a disorder of:
questions.why: Orotic aciduria is a defect of pyrimidine biosynthesis.

questions.stem: The copper-transport protein defective in Menkes disease is:
questions.why: Menkes disease is an X-linked defect of the ATP7A copper transporter.
